content.title: About
content.content: Crepe with meat is a thin batter made from flour, eggs, milk and a small amount of butter, rolled around a thin layer of boiled or fried meat. The crepe has a delicate texture while the meat filling adds a rich flavor and extra nutritional value.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Crepes are prepared in many world cuisines: French crêpes, Russian blini, Italian frittatas.
In Russia, meat‑filled crepes are often served with sour cream or tomato sauce.
The thin batter cooks quickly, usually 1–2 minutes per side.
Meat fillings can be beef, pork, chicken or turkey, depending on regional preferences.
Crepes are a popular dish for celebrations, such as Maslenitsa.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The meat filling provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat supplies vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from the meat helps form hemoglobin and prevents anemia.

items.title: Balanced carbohydrates
items.content: Whole‑grain flour in the batter offers slow‑release energy.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and complex carbs helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Using a lot of butter or fatty meat can make the dish calorie‑dense.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat flour contains gluten, which may trigger reactions in people with celiac disease.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Meat must be fully cooked to avoid salmonella or campylobacter contamination.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Added salt in the batter or filling can be a concern for those with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the crepe hot, folded into a pocket or rolled. Top with sour cream, tomato sauce, fresh herbs or grated cheese. It pairs well with a side salad or mashed potatoes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked crepes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in a skillet or microwave. Frozen crepes keep their quality for up to 1 month.

content.title: About
content.content: Margarita is a classic cocktail made of tequila, lime juice, and orange liqueur (triple sec or Cointreau). It is served in a glass with a salt‑rimmed edge and often garnished with a lime wedge. The drink originated in Mexico in the mid‑20th century and quickly gained worldwide popularity.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recorded Margarita recipe dates back to the 1930s in Tijuana, Mexico.
There are many variations, including fruit‑puree versions, berry twists, or swapping tequila for rum (known as a "Tommy Jerry").
The traditional salt rim can be replaced with sugar, spices, or a salt‑and‑chili mix for extra heat.
Margarita is often considered a celebratory drink and is served at parties, weddings, and bars worldwide.
In the United States during the 1970s, Margarita became the best‑selling cocktail in restaurants.

items.title: Vitamin C from lime
items.content: Lime juice is rich in vitamin C, which supports the immune system and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Beneficial plant compounds
items.content: Tequila, derived from agave, contains small amounts of polyphenols that may have anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Moderate consumption may promote relaxation
items.content: Alcohol in moderate amounts can help reduce stress and improve mood.

items.title: Alcohol content
items.content: Margarita contains alcohol, so it should be consumed responsibly, avoided before driving, and is not recommended for pregnant individuals or those with liver disease.

items.title: Salt rim
items.content: The salted rim adds sodium, which may be undesirable for people with hypertension.

items.title: Lime acidity
items.content: The acidity can irritate sensitive stomachs and cause heartburn.

items.title: Allergies to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to tequila (agave) or to orange liqueur.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Serve Margarita in a salt‑rimmed glass, garnish with a lime wedge. For a frozen version, blend the ingredients with ice until smooth. To lighten the drink, reduce the amount of tequila and increase lime juice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Alcoholic components (tequila, liqueur) should be kept in tightly sealed bottles in a cool, dark place. Fresh lime juice is best used immediately, but can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 2 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Mousse is a light, airy dessert made from whipped egg whites, cream, sugar and flavorings. It can be sweet or savory and is often used in pastry arts to create elegant dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first mousse recipes appeared in France in the 19th century.
There are more than 30 mousse varieties: chocolate, fruit, caramel, cheese and even vegetable.
Gelatin or agar‑agar is often added to achieve the perfect fluffy texture.
Mousse can be served cold or slightly warmed, depending on the recipe.
Traditional chocolate mousse is made without eggs, using only cream and melted chocolate.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Egg whites used in mousse provide a high‑quality source of protein.

items.title: Low in fat (when using reduced‑fat cream)
items.content: Light versions of mousse can be low‑calorie if part of the cream is replaced with reduced‑fat alternatives.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain vitamin B12, riboflavin and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Contains calcium
items.content: Cream used in the recipe is a good source of calcium, supporting bone health.

items.title: Antioxidants from flavorings
items.content: Fruit and chocolate add‑ins are often rich in polyphenols, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Mousse made with egg whites can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet mousses frequently contain high amounts of sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: If not kept at proper temperature, mousse made with raw eggs can become a breeding ground for pathogens.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Classic mousse based on cream contains saturated fats and should be consumed in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve mousse in individual glasses or dessert plates. Pair it with berries, fruit coulis, nuts, chocolate shavings or mint. For a lighter version, use reduced‑fat cream and sugar substitutes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared mousse in the refrigerator in a sealed container for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container for up to 1 month. Before serving, allow the mousse to thaw slightly and give it a gentle stir.

content.title: About
content.content: Nectarine is a juicy stone fruit from the Rosaceae family, closely related to peaches. Raw nectarine offers a sweet‑tart flavor and tender, juicy flesh. It is typically eaten fresh and used in salads, desserts, and smoothies.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Nectarines originated in Asia but are now cultivated in many warm regions worldwide.
Unlike peaches, nectarines have smooth skin without fuzz.
The harvest season in the Northern Hemisphere usually runs from late May through August.
Nectarines are rich in antioxidants, including vitamin C and carotenoids.
Several cultivars exist, varying in flesh color from white to bright orange.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Carotenoids and flavonoids help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in nectarine promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium assists in fluid balance and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Low‑calorie snack
items.content: Nectarine is low in calories, making it a good choice for weight management.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to nectarine.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Choose organic fruit or wash thoroughly to reduce pesticide exposure.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: People with diabetes should consider the fruit’s glycemic impact and monitor portion size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw nectarine is eaten whole after washing. It can be sliced into salads, added to yogurt, blended into smoothies, or used in baking. The skin is edible, but can be peeled if preferred.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store nectarines at room temperature until fully ripe, then refrigerate where they stay fresh for up to 5 days. Avoid airtight containers to prevent moisture buildup.

pizza-with-beans-and-vegetables-thin-cru.title: Pizza with beans and vegetables, thin crust

content.title: About
content.content: A thin, crispy pizza topped with tomato sauce, quality beans, fresh vegetables (bell pepper, onion, zucchini, tomatoes) and a light layer of mozzarella cheese. A perfect choice for a light yet satisfying vegetarian snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beans boost the plant‑based protein and fiber content of the pizza.
Thin crust is baked without added oil, reducing calories compared with traditional pizza.
The vegetables used are rich in vitamins A, C, and K.
Tomato sauce provides lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.
Bean‑topped pizza is a common Mediterranean alternative to meat‑based pies.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Beans deliver about 7 g of protein per serving, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes lasting satiety.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Thin crust and modest cheese amount make this pizza more heart‑friendly.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vegetables supply vitamin C, potassium, and folate, important for immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Tomato sauce and vegetables contain lycopene and carotenoids that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce and cheese can increase sodium levels; those monitoring blood pressure should choose a low‑salt version.

items.title: Gluten in crust
items.content: Thin crust is typically wheat‑based; people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should look for a gluten‑free alternative.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Reheat the pizza in a 180 °C oven for 5‑7 minutes until the crust is crisp. Optionally top with fresh arugula or basil after heating.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked pizza in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in freezer‑safe bags for up to 1 month. Thaw in the fridge before reheating.

rice-brown-with-vegetables-cheese-and-or.title: Brown Rice with Vegetables, Cheese and/or Cream Sauce, Fat Added

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice with vegetables, cheese and/or cream sauce is a dish that combines whole‑grain rice, a mix of vegetables (such as carrots, broccoli, bell pepper) and a sauce made from cheese and/or cream with added fat. It provides complex carbohydrates, fiber, B‑vitamins, vitamin C, calcium and protein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains the bran and germ, giving it more fiber and nutrients than white rice.
Vegetables add color, flavor and a boost of antioxidants.
Cheese sauce supplies calcium and vitamin D when made with fortified cheese.
Added fat (oil, cream) enhances absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins from the vegetables.
The dish is common in Asian and Mediterranean cuisines as a hearty lunch or dinner.

items.title: Supports Digestion
items.content: Fiber from whole‑grain rice and vegetables promotes regular bowel movements and prevents constipation.

items.title: Stabilizes Blood Sugar
items.content: Complex carbs in brown rice release glucose slowly, helping maintain steady blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Strengthens Bones
items.content: Calcium from the cheese sauce and vitamin D contribute to bone health.

items.title: Boosts Immunity
items.content: Vitamin C from vegetables and antioxidants help reinforce the immune system.

items.title: Provides Sustained Energy
items.content: Fats and protein in the sauce give lasting satiety and energy.

items.title: Dairy Allergy
items.content: Cheese and cream sauces can trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: High Calorie Content
items.content: Added fat increases the dish’s calorie density, so portion control is important for weight‑managed diets.

items.title: Sodium Levels
items.content: Cheeses often contain salt; choose low‑sodium or reduced‑fat varieties if you have hypertension.

items.title: Food Interactions
items.content: Large amounts of fat may slow the absorption of certain medications; keep a time gap when taking drugs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a main course or side. Garnish with fresh herbs (parsley, dill) for extra aroma. For a lighter version, replace part of the fat with olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat gently and add a splash of water or milk to loosen the sauce.
